title: The flood of new writing: Gray Suede, Key F and Dalvatore
summary: Once the block lifted the pieces poured out, and he regrets that others turned them into suites.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Did you go directly back to Boyd?

Well, when Harry damaged himself punching through a plate glass window, I rejoined Boyd and that's when it happened; that's when I wrote "There's No You" and had this new vision, this new understanding, new feeling when writing.
How long did it take from that first chart to get into doing "Gray Suede" and "Key F" and "Dalvatore?"

They just poured out of me, everything started to pour out of me at that point. It was as if I had found the thing in me that was blocking whatever creativity there was in me, presenting it and the minute I found the thing and removed it, it just gushed out. I couldn't--it was hard to stop, it just kept coming and coming and coming. It was hard to do simple things, because I just wanted to keep writing. I began to realize that you don't do it all in one piece of music. If you are patient with yourself, get to know yourself a little better, you pace yourself, and so all these things began to happen.
Did you begin to feel particularly constrained then with three minute records or was that so ingrained?
That's a point; it mustn't have bothered me, because I didn't give
it any thought. These were fences that I couldn't knock down.

It occurred to me that if there was any justification at all for calling these a suite, it was because you really had something more to say than one three minute segment and by making it a suite, you could have some kind of continuity.
Right! that's true, but of course none of that was my doing. That was done for me or to me and others made these decisions. They were done when I wasn't around; this is what bothered me.
